newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's slowing growth worries Banque Audi.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's slowing growth worries Banque Audi.

text.p: Lebanon's economic growth slowed in the first nine months of 1996 and there are no significant signs of a quick recovery, Banque Audi said in its third-quarter report on the economy released on Tuesday.

Lack of peace in the Middle East meant Lebanon had to rely on its own efforts to create wealth and employment, and to do that the government had to win over people to its policies by introducing reforms aimed at improving their well-being, it said.
"It is only together and looking ahead that we can overcome pessimism," the bank said.
The estimated annual growth rate fell to four percent in the first nine months of 1996 from 6.5 percent in the same period of 1995, the report said.
Growth of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) continued in the third quarter at the same rate as in the first two, it said.
"Following a promising year in 1995, the Lebanese economy has witnessed a slowdown in 1996, with perspectives that do not reveal significant recovery signs soon," the report said.
Banque Audi is one of Lebanon's leading commercial banks and the reports prepared by its economic analysis unit are well regarded in financial and business circles.

It attributed the slowdown to three factors: Israel's 17-day blitz on Lebanon in April, an austere budgetary policy which caused a 10.3 percent drop in public investment during the period, and the crowding-out effects of the goverment's restrictive monetary policy.
The government's budgetary policy, while rigorous enough to hinder growth, was not rigorous enough to restore fiscal balance and credibility, Banque Audi said.

The crowding-out effect -- caused by high interest rates on Lebanese pound-denominated treasury bills which finance the budget deficit -- meant the public sector had a 45.7 percent share of total bank credits, depriving the private sector of substantial financing resources, it said.
"Private investment has significantly slowed down and the other components of demand have not recaptured the needed amounts," it added.
Banque Audi said the government was facing a dilemma: "It has at the same time to stimulate the economy and reduce (budget) deficits. Are the two objectives compatible?"
While financial markets appeared unworried by the contradiction, the government was facing tensions on the social front because its policies were contributing to slowing down economic activity.

The two elements needed to favour development were public confidence in the government and regional political stability. The latter was lacking and without it Lebanon had to rely on its own efforts to create wealth and employment, particularly through its small and medium enterprises, the report said.
"After having convinced the markets (of its policies), the government should try to convince the politicians and the Lebanese at large," it added.

"The message should be clear: the time has come for reforms to materialise. The ministers should be first and foremost concerned about the well-being of the Lebanese. They have to implement...measures to concretely improve the daily life of citizens," Banque Audi said.
